A consumable sample is first introduced into a first chamber of a test container. The sample may be any food, beverage, or other consumable material to be evaluated for the presence of an allergen. Once received in the first chamber, the consumable sample is processed to convert it into a homogenized sample. This processing may include mechanical disruption, mixing, grinding, agitation, or another suitable technique that breaks down the sample and distributes its components more uniformly.

After homogenization, the homogenized sample is delivered from the first chamber to a second chamber of the test container. In the second chamber, the homogenized sample is combined with a process reagent. The process reagent interacts with the homogenized sample to produce a dispersion, which helps suspend or release target substances, including any allergen that may be present, in a form suitable for subsequent analysis.

A selected volume of the resulting dispersion is then transmitted from the second chamber to an analysis chamber. The analysis chamber is positioned to receive the dispersion from an outlet port of the second chamber and includes a detection substrate located near that outlet port. As the dispersion enters or contacts the analysis chamber, it encounters the detection substrate, which is configured to react with, bind to, or otherwise indicate the presence of the target allergen.

An optical sensor is arranged to observe the analysis chamber through a detection window. The optical sensor detects optical signals associated with the detection substrate, such as changes in color, fluorescence, absorbance, reflectance, or another measurable optical characteristic. Based on the detected signals, the system determines whether the allergen is present in the original consumable sample.
outputs.L4:
A system and method are provided for detecting allergens, contaminants, or other harmful substances in a consumable sample, such as food, beverages, supplements, or similar ingestible products. The system is designed to prepare and analyze the sample within an integrated container, reducing the need for separate laboratory equipment and minimizing the risk of sample loss or cross-contamination during handling.

In use, a portion of the consumable sample is introduced into a sample-processing region of the container. The sample is then homogenized, macerated, crushed, shaken, stirred, or otherwise mechanically processed so that any target substance present in the sample is released and distributed throughout the mixture. A reagent is added to the processed sample to form a dispersion. The reagent may include one or more chemical, biochemical, enzymatic, immunological, or binding components selected to interact with a target allergen or harmful substance. Examples of detectable targets may include peanut proteins, tree nut proteins, gluten, milk proteins, egg proteins, soy proteins, shellfish residues, toxins, pathogens, chemical contaminants, or other substances that may be unsafe or undesirable for consumption.

After the sample and reagent are combined, the resulting dispersion is transferred from the sample-processing region to an analysis chamber. The transfer may occur through a passage, valve, membrane, channel, or other fluid-routing structure within the same container. The analysis chamber includes a detection substrate configured to receive the dispersion and produce a measurable response when the target substance is present. The detection substrate may be a test strip, membrane, coated surface, microfluidic assay region, biosensor surface, or other reactive material. In some embodiments, the substrate contains antibodies, aptamers, binding proteins, indicator dyes, fluorescent markers, colorimetric reagents, nanoparticles, or other detection elements that generate an optical signal in response to the target substance.

The analysis chamber includes a detection window positioned so that an optical sensor can read the signal produced by the detection substrate without opening the container. The detection window may be transparent or translucent and may be formed from glass, plastic, or another optically suitable material. The optical sensor may detect changes in color, fluorescence, absorbance, reflectance, luminescence, or another optical characteristic associated with the reaction between the target substance and the detection substrate. Based on the measured optical signal, the system determines whether the allergen or harmful substance is present, absent, or present above a threshold concentration.

The system may include processing electronics or may communicate with an external device, such as a handheld reader, smartphone, tablet, or dedicated analyzer. The measured optical signal may be compared with stored calibration data, control signals, reference values, or threshold levels to generate a result. The result may be displayed to a user as a simple indication, such as “detected” or “not detected,” or as a quantitative or semi-quantitative measurement of concentration. The system may also include a control region to verify that the reagent, detection substrate, and fluid transfer steps have functioned properly.

By integrating sample homogenization, reagent mixing, fluid transfer, and optical detection within a single container, the system provides an efficient and convenient approach for testing consumable products. The closed or partially closed configuration helps reduce user exposure to the sample and reagent, limits contamination, and simplifies operation. The method may be performed at the point of use, such as in homes, restaurants, food-processing facilities, schools, hospitals, or retail environments, enabling rapid screening of consumable samples for allergens or harmful substances before consumption or distribution.

A system is a set of connected parts that work together to achieve a purpose. It can be simple, like a routine for organizing daily tasks, or complex, like a computer network, a business process, or an ecosystem. What makes a system effective is the way its parts interact. Each element has a role, and when those roles are clear, the whole system becomes more reliable and efficient.

A system also depends on balance. If one part stops working or becomes overloaded, the entire structure may be affected. For example, in a company, communication, planning, production, and customer service all influence one another. If communication fails, decisions may be delayed, mistakes may increase, and results may suffer.

Good systems are designed to solve problems, reduce confusion, and create consistency. They help people understand what needs to be done, how it should be done, and who is responsible. Whether in technology, education, healthcare, or everyday life, a strong system supports better organization and smarter decisions.

In the end, a system and its components must work together smoothly. When they do, they create order, improve performance, and make goals easier to reach.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent claim for a system and method that detects allergens or harmful substances in a food sample using a multi-chamber test container, reagent mixing, a detection substrate, and an optical sensor.
counterfactuals.output:
Below is a draft set of patent-style claims covering both a **system** and a **method** for detecting allergens or harmful substances in a food sample using a multi-chamber test container, reagent mixing, a detection substrate, and an optical sensor.

---

## Claims

### 1. System Claim

1. **A system for detecting an allergen or harmful substance in a food sample, the system comprising:**

   a multi-chamber test container comprising:  
   - a sample chamber configured to receive the food sample;  
   - at least one reagent chamber containing one or more reagents configured to react with the allergen or harmful substance;  
   - a mixing chamber fluidically connectable to the sample chamber and the at least one reagent chamber; and  
   - a detection chamber comprising a detection substrate;

   a fluid control mechanism configured to selectively transfer the food sample and the one or more reagents between the sample chamber, the at least one reagent chamber, the mixing chamber, and the detection chamber;

   wherein the detection substrate is configured to produce an optically detectable change in response to presence of the allergen or harmful substance or a reaction product thereof; and

   an optical sensor positioned to detect the optically detectable change from the detection substrate and generate a detection signal indicative of presence, absence, or concentration of the allergen or harmful substance in the food sample.

---

### 2. Dependent Claims

2. The system of claim 1, wherein the allergen comprises at least one of peanut protein, tree nut protein, milk protein, egg protein, soy protein, wheat protein, fish protein, shellfish protein, sesame protein, or gluten.

3. The system of claim 1, wherein the harmful substance comprises at least one of a toxin, pesticide residue, heavy metal, bacterial contaminant, fungal contaminant, viral contaminant, chemical adulterant, or environmental contaminant.

4. The system of claim 1, wherein the one or more reagents comprise an antibody, aptamer, enzyme, nucleic acid probe, colorimetric reagent, fluorescent reagent, chemiluminescent reagent, nanoparticle conjugate, or binding ligand specific to the allergen or harmful substance.

5. The system of claim 1, wherein the detection substrate comprises a lateral flow membrane, porous membrane, hydrogel, microarray surface, coated polymer film, functionalized glass surface, functionalized plastic surface, or immobilized capture reagent.

6. The system of claim 1, wherein the optically detectable change comprises a change in color, fluorescence, luminescence, absorbance, reflectance, scattering, or optical density.

7. The system of claim 1, wherein the optical sensor comprises a photodiode, phototransistor, camera, CMOS image sensor, CCD sensor, spectrometer, color sensor, fluorescence detector, or reflectance sensor.

8. The system of claim 1, further comprising a processor configured to compare the detection signal to a stored threshold or calibration curve and output a result indicating presence, absence, or concentration of the allergen or harmful substance.

9. The system of claim 8, further comprising a user interface configured to display the result to a user.

10. The system of claim 1, wherein the fluid control mechanism comprises at least one of a frangible seal, valve, membrane, plunger, pump, squeeze-actuated chamber, capillary channel, centrifugal flow structure, or pressure-actuated passage.

11. The system of claim 1, wherein the multi-chamber test container is a disposable cartridge configured for insertion into a reusable reader containing the optical sensor.

12. The system of claim 1, wherein at least one reagent chamber stores a dry reagent and the sample chamber or another chamber stores or receives a liquid configured to rehydrate the dry reagent.

13. The system of claim 1, wherein the mixing chamber includes a mixing feature comprising at least one of a baffle, bead, textured surface, serpentine channel, membrane, or agitation region.

14. The system of claim 1, wherein the detection substrate includes a control region configured to generate a control optical signal indicating proper operation of the system.

15. The system of claim 1, wherein the optical sensor is configured to detect a spatial pattern on the detection substrate corresponding to a plurality of different allergens or harmful substances.

---

### 3. Method Claim

16. **A method for detecting an allergen or harmful substance in a food sample, the method comprising:**

   introducing the food sample into a sample chamber of a multi-chamber test container;

   transferring at least a portion of the food sample from the sample chamber into a mixing chamber;

   releasing one or more reagents from at least one reagent chamber into the mixing chamber;

   mixing the portion of the food sample with the one or more reagents to form a reaction mixture;

   transferring the reaction mixture to a detection chamber comprising a detection substrate;

   generating, at the detection substrate, an optically detectable change in response to presence of the allergen or harmful substance or a reaction product thereof;

   detecting the optically detectable change using an optical sensor; and

   determining, based on an output of the optical sensor, presence, absence, or concentration of the allergen or harmful substance in the food sample.

---

### 4. Dependent Method Claims

17. The method of claim 16, wherein determining the presence, absence, or concentration comprises comparing the output of the optical sensor to a predetermined threshold or calibration curve.

18. The method of claim 16, wherein the optically detectable change comprises a colorimetric, fluorescent, chemiluminescent, absorbance, reflectance, or scattering change.

19. The method of claim 16, further comprising filtering or homogenizing the food sample before transferring the portion of the food sample into the mixing chamber.

20. The method of claim 16, further comprising incubating the reaction mixture in the mixing chamber for a predetermined time before transferring the reaction mixture to the detection chamber.

21. The method of claim 16, further comprising reading a control region of the detection substrate to verify validity of the detection.

22. The method of claim 16, wherein releasing the one or more reagents comprises rupturing a frangible seal, opening a valve, compressing a chamber, actuating a plunger, or applying centrifugal force.

23. The method of claim 16, wherein the optical sensor captures an image of the detection substrate and a processor analyzes intensity, color, spatial location, or spectral response of the image.

24. The method of claim 16, further comprising displaying a result on a user interface or transmitting the result to a remote computing device.

25. The method of claim 16, wherein the method detects a plurality of allergens or harmful substances using a plurality of detection regions on the detection substrate.

---

### 5. Additional Broad Independent Claim

26. **A disposable test cartridge for detecting an allergen or harmful substance in a food sample, the disposable test cartridge comprising:**

   a housing defining a plurality of chambers including a sample chamber, a reagent chamber, a mixing chamber, and a detection chamber;

   one or more fluid passages selectively connecting the plurality of chambers;

   one or more reagents disposed in the reagent chamber and configured to bind to or react with the allergen or harmful substance;

   a detection substrate disposed in the detection chamber and including at least one capture or reaction region configured to generate an optical response when exposed to a mixture of the food sample and the one or more reagents; and

   an optical window aligned with the detection substrate and configured to permit an external optical reader to detect the optical response.

---

*This draft is for general drafting assistance only and should be reviewed and tailored by a qualified patent professional based on the specific invention, prior art, jurisdiction, and desired claim scope.*

counterfactuals.output:
A method is provided for detecting the presence of one or more allergenic substances in a consumable sample using a test container configured for sample processing and optical detection.

In one embodiment, the method comprises introducing a consumable sample into a test container having a body defining a plurality of fluidically connectable chambers. The plurality of chambers may include, for example, a sample receiving chamber, a reagent or extraction chamber, and a detection chamber. The test container further comprises at least one port configured to permit introduction of the sample, a liquid reagent, or both, and a detection substrate disposed at or near the port or in fluid communication with the port. The detection substrate may comprise an immunoassay strip, membrane, pad, lateral-flow substrate, porous matrix, microfluidic substrate, or other carrier bearing one or more allergen-specific binding agents. The test container further includes a detection window positioned to permit optical interrogation of at least a portion of the detection substrate or a reaction zone associated therewith.

The method may include placing the consumable sample into the sample receiving chamber through the port and combining the sample with an extraction fluid, buffer, solvent, or reagent contained in, or introduced into, one of the chambers. The sample may be mixed, agitated, compressed, filtered, incubated, or otherwise treated within the test container to release or solubilize allergenic components. In certain embodiments, fluid communication between chambers is selectively established by opening a valve, rupturing a frangible seal, deforming a wall of the container, rotating or sliding a component of the container, or applying pressure to one or more chambers.

Following sample preparation, at least a portion of the treated sample is transferred from a first chamber to a second chamber and then to the detection substrate. Transfer may occur by gravity, capillary action, pressure differential, manual squeezing, wicking, pump action, or another fluid-driving mechanism. As the treated sample contacts the detection substrate, allergen molecules or allergen-associated epitopes, if present, bind to one or more capture or detection reagents provided on the substrate. The binding event may produce an optically detectable response, including but not limited to a colorimetric, fluorescent, chemiluminescent, scattering, absorbance, reflectance, or transmission-based signal.

The detection substrate may include one or more test zones corresponding to different allergens, allergen classes, or allergen-derived proteins. Exemplary allergens detectable by the method include peanut, tree nut, milk, egg, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, sesame, gluten-containing grain components, or combinations thereof. The substrate may further include a control zone configured to indicate proper fluid migration, reagent activity, assay validity, or sufficient sample volume.

The method further comprises optically sensing the detection substrate through the detection window. Optical sensing may be performed visually by a user or by an optical reader comprising a light source, imaging sensor, photodiode, camera, spectrometer, or other detection element. In some embodiments, the optical reader is incorporated into a handheld device, a dedicated analyzer, or a mobile computing device. The optical reader may illuminate the detection substrate through the detection window and measure an optical characteristic of one or more test zones. The measured optical characteristic may be compared with a threshold, calibration value, reference region, or control response to determine the presence, absence, or approximate concentration of the allergen in the consumable sample.

In certain embodiments, the detection window comprises a transparent or translucent portion of the test container aligned with the detection substrate. The detection window may be formed from glass, polymer, film, or another optically transmissive material and may be configured to reduce contamination, evaporation, or user exposure to reagents while permitting optical interrogation of the detection substrate. The detection window may include alignment features, fiducial marks, magnifying regions, optical filters, or indexing structures to assist in positioning the reader relative to the test zones.

The method may further include generating an output indicative of the allergen detection result. The output may include a positive indication, a negative indication, an invalid-test indication, a quantitative concentration value, a semi-quantitative allergen level, or a warning signal. In embodiments using an electronic reader, the output may be displayed, stored, transmitted, or associated with sample-identifying information. The method may also include determining whether the consumable sample is suitable for ingestion by a particular individual based on the detected allergen result.

In one exemplary sequence, a food or beverage sample is placed into the receiving chamber of the test container. An extraction reagent is released from a reagent chamber into the receiving chamber and mixed with the sample. The resulting liquid extract is directed through a filter or passage into the detection chamber. The extract contacts a detection substrate positioned near the port and aligned with the detection window. Allergen-specific binding occurs on the detection substrate, producing a visible or optically measurable signal at one or more test regions. The signal is observed through the detection window and interpreted to indicate whether the consumable sample contains a target allergen.

The described method enables contained sample handling, integrated reagent processing, and optical allergen detection within a multi-chamber test container, thereby reducing cross-contamination risk and facilitating rapid analysis of consumable samples at a point of use.
